# Draft:Motorways in the United Kingdom

Motorways in the United Kingdom form the highest‑standard roads in the national network, designed to support long‑distance, high‑speed travel between major cities, regions, and economic centres. First introduced in the late 1950s, the system has expanded into a network spanning England, Scotland, and Wales, characterised by controlled access, grade‑separated junctions, and regulated traffic rules. Motorways are identified by the prefix M or by upgraded sections of primary routes carrying an (M) designation.
The network plays a central role in the UK’s transport infrastructure, carrying a significant proportion of national road traffic despite representing a small share of total road length. Over time, it has evolved to include smart motorway technology, variable speed limits, and active traffic management aimed at improving safety and reducing congestion. Today, UK motorways remain essential for freight movement, commuter travel, and regional connectivity across the country.
Motorways have the highest speed limit in the country, 70mph (112kph), some sections have lower permanent speed limits, and some motorways, known as smart motorways, have temporary speed limits they can impose in the event of a hazard. Motorways never had speed limits, until 1965, where they imposed the first speed limits, at 70mph (112kph), which they still are to this day.
